reference.source: Rutherford's Vascular Surgery and Endovascular Therapy
clinicalPearls: The most common form of primary lymphoedema, defined by onset around puberty and before the age of 35 years, hence the alternative term lymphoedema praecox.
It shows a clear female predominance and typically presents as bilateral, often asymmetrical, lower-limb swelling.
Inheritance is usually autosomal dominant with variable penetrance and expressivity, so an affected first-degree relative supports the diagnosis.
It is distinguished from Milroy disease, which is congenital, type I and classically linked to FLT4 (VEGFR3) mutations, whereas Meige disease presents later and is genetically heterogeneous.
By definition Meige disease is isolated lymphoedema; the presence of distichiasis points instead to FOXC2-related lymphoedema-distichiasis and warrants ophthalmic examination.
The Stemmer sign is positive and the swelling begins distally before ascending, becoming progressively less pitting over time.
As with all chronic lymphoedema, recurrent cellulitis is common and both worsens and is worsened by the underlying lymphatic failure.
Lymphoscintigraphy confirms impaired lymphatic transport and helps exclude a secondary cause when onset is unusually asymmetrical or abrupt.
reference.pathophysiology: Meige lymphoedema arises from a constitutional abnormality of the peripheral lymphatic vessels, most often hypoplasia or aplasia of the collecting lymphatics, which becomes clinically manifest around puberty. The peripubertal timing suggests a hormonal trigger that unmasks marginal lymphatic reserve. Deficient lymphatic drainage causes accumulation of protein-rich interstitial fluid, and the resulting chronic inflammation drives adipose deposition and dermal fibrosis in the same self-perpetuating manner seen across primary lymphoedema. The condition is genetically heterogeneous, and it must be separated from defined single-gene entities such as FOXC2-related lymphoedema-distichiasis and GJC2-associated disease, which have distinct features and inheritance.
additionalDifferentials: Milroy disease (congenital hereditary lymphoedema type I)
lymphoedema tarda with onset after 35 years
secondary lymphoedema from infection, malignancy or trauma
systemic oedema from cardiac, renal or hepatic disease
additionalInvestigations: lymphoscintigraphy to demonstrate impaired lymphatic transport
detailed family pedigree and targeted genetic testing
venous duplex ultrasonography to exclude venous disease
MR or CT lymphangiography for anatomical assessment
slit-lamp ophthalmic examination to exclude distichiasis
thyroid, renal, hepatic and cardiac evaluation to exclude systemic oedema
redFlags: new violaceous or haemorrhagic cutaneous nodules suggesting angiosarcoma
rapidly progressive or newly asymmetrical swelling prompting exclusion of malignancy
syndromic features such as distichiasis, ptosis or yellow nails indicating an alternative diagnosis
reference.prognosis: Meige lymphoedema is a lifelong condition, but with compression, skin care, exercise and infection prevention most patients maintain good limb function and a favourable quality of life. The outlook worsens with recurrent cellulitis and advanced fibrosis, and the small long-term risk of angiosarcoma persists.
pitfalls: labelling all pubertal-onset lymphoedema as isolated Meige disease without checking for distichiasis or other syndromic features
failing to take a family history and thereby missing the hereditary pattern
undertreating cellulitis and accelerating lymphatic damage
attributing swelling to venous disease and delaying appropriate lymphatic management
references: Rutherford's Vascular Surgery and Endovascular Therapy
Browse's Introduction to the Symptoms and Signs of Surgical Disease
International Society of Lymphology Consensus Document on the diagnosis and treatment of peripheral lymphoedema
management: Deliver complete decongestive therapy with multilayer bandaging and graduated compression garments as the mainstay
Maintain meticulous skin care and hygiene to preserve the skin barrier and reduce infection risk
Treat cellulitis promptly with antibiotics and offer antibiotic prophylaxis for recurrent episodes
Encourage exercise, limb elevation and weight optimisation to support lymphatic drainage
Provide manual lymphatic drainage and consider surgery such as lymphaticovenous anastomosis, vascularised lymph node transfer or debulking in selected refractory cases
Exclude systemic causes of oedema and defined single-gene entities such as FOXC2-related lymphoedema-distichiasis
Offer genetic counselling given the autosomal dominant inheritance with variable penetrance
Undertake long-term surveillance for advancing fibrosis and the rare long-term risk of angiosarcoma
